source: Stubb was the second mate. He was a native of Cape Cod; and hence, according to local usage, was called a Cape-Cod-man. A happy-go-lucky; neither craven nor valiant; taking perils as they came with an indifferent air; and while engaged in the most imminent crisis of the chase, toiling away, calm and collected as a journeyman joiner engaged for the year. Good-humored, easy, and careless, he presided over his whale-boat as if the most deadly encounter were but a dinner, and his crew all invited guests. He was as particular about the comfortable arrangement of his part of the boat, as an old stage-driver is about the snugness of his box. When close to the whale, in the very death-lock of the fight, he handled his unpitying lance coolly and off-handedly, as a whistling tinker his hammer. He would hum over his old rigadig tunes while flank and flank with the most exasperated monster. Long usage had, for this Stubb, converted the jaws of death into an easy chair. What he thought of death itself, there is no telling. Whether he ever thought of it at all, might be a question; but, if he ever did chance to cast his mind that way after a comfortable dinner, no doubt, like a good sailor, he took it to be a sort of call of the watch to tumble aloft, and bestir themselves there, about something which he would find out when he obeyed the order, and not sooner.

What, perhaps, with other things, made Stubb such an easy-going, unfearing man, so cheerily trudging off with the burden of life in a world full of grave pedlars, all bowed to the ground with their packs; what helped to bring about that almost impious good-humor of his; that thing must have been his pipe. For, like his nose, his short, black little pipe was one of the regular features of his face. You would almost as soon have expected him to turn out of his bunk without his nose as without his pipe. He kept a whole row of pipes there ready loaded, stuck in a rack, within easy reach of his hand; and, whenever he turned in, he smoked them all out in succession, lighting one from the other to the end of the chapter; then loading them again to be in readiness anew. For, when Stubb dressed, instead of first putting his legs into his trowsers, he put his pipe into his mouth.

I say this continual smoking must have been one cause, at least, of his peculiar disposition; for every one knows that this earthly air, whether ashore or afloat, is terribly infected with the nameless miseries of the numberless mortals who have died exhaling it; and as in time of the cholera, some people go about with a camphorated handkerchief to their mouths; so, likewise, against all mortal tribulations, Stubb’s tobacco smoke might have operated as a sort of disinfecting agent.

The third mate was Flask, a native of Tisbury, in Martha’s Vineyard. A short, stout, ruddy young fellow, very pugnacious concerning whales, who somehow seemed to think that the great leviathans had personally and hereditarily affronted him; and therefore it was a sort of point of honor with him, to destroy them whenever encountered. So utterly lost was he to all sense of reverence for the many marvels of their majestic bulk and mystic ways; and so dead to anything like an apprehension of any possible danger from encountering them; that in his poor opinion, the wondrous whale was but a species of magnified mouse, or at least water-rat, requiring only a little circumvention and some small application of time and trouble in order to kill and boil. This ignorant, unconscious fearlessness of his made him a little waggish in the matter of whales; he followed these fish for the fun of it; and a three years’ voyage round Cape Horn was only a jolly joke that lasted that length of time. As a carpenter’s nails are divided into wrought nails and cut nails; so mankind may be similarly divided. Little Flask was one of the wrought ones; made to clinch tight and last long. They called him King-Post on board of the Pequod; because, in form, he could be well likened to the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers; and which by the means of many radiating side timbers inserted into it, serves to brace the ship against the icy concussions of those battering seas.

Now these three mates—Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask, were momentous men. They it was who by universal prescription commanded three of the Pequod’s boats as headsmen. In that grand order of battle in which Captain Ahab would probably marshal his forces to descend on the whales, these three headsmen were as captains of companies. Or, being armed with their long keen whaling spears, they were as a picked trio of lancers; even as the harpooneers were flingers of javelins.

And since in this famous fishery, each mate or headsman, like a Gothic Knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooneer, who in certain conjunctures provides him with a fresh lance, when the former one has been badly twisted, or elbowed in the assault; and moreover, as there generally subsists between the two, a close intimacy and friendliness; it is therefore but meet, that in this place we set down who the Pequod’s harpooneers were, and to what headsman each of them belonged.
First of all was Queequeg, whom Starbuck, the chief mate, had selected for his squire. But Queequeg is already known.

Next was Tashtego, an unmixed Indian from Gay Head, the most westerly promontory of Martha’s Vineyard, where there still exists the last remnant of a village of red men, which has long supplied the neighboring island of Nantucket with many of her most daring harpooneers. In the fishery, they usually go by the generic name of Gay-Headers. Tashtego’s long, lean, sable hair, his high cheek bones, and black rounding eyes—for an Indian, Oriental in their largeness, but Antarctic in their glittering expression—all this sufficiently proclaimed him an inheritor of the unvitiated blood of those proud warrior hunters, who, in quest of the great New England moose, had scoured, bow in hand, the aboriginal forests of the main. But no longer snuffing in the trail of the wild beasts of the woodland, Tashtego now hunted in the wake of the great whales of the sea; the unerring harpoon of the son fitly replacing the infallible arrow of the sires. To look at the tawny brawn of his lithe snaky limbs, you would almost have credited the superstitions of some of the earlier Puritans, and half-believed this wild Indian to be a son of the Prince of the Powers of the Air. Tashtego was Stubb the second mate’s squire.

Third among the harpooneers was Daggoo, a gigantic, coal-black negro-savage, with a lion-like tread—an Ahasuerus to behold. Suspended from his ears were two golden hoops, so large that the sailors called them ring-bolts, and would talk of securing the top-sail halyards to them. In his youth Daggoo had voluntarily shipped on board of a whaler, lying in a lonely bay on his native coast. And never having been anywhere in the world but in Africa, Nantucket, and the pagan harbors most frequented by whalemen; and having now led for many years the bold life of the fishery in the ships of owners uncommonly heedful of what manner of men they shipped; Daggoo retained all his barbaric virtues, and erect as a giraffe, moved about the decks in all the pomp of six feet five in his socks. There was a corporeal humility in looking up at him; and a white man standing before him seemed a white flag come to beg truce of a fortress. Curious to tell, this imperial negro, Ahasuerus Daggoo, was the Squire of little Flask, who looked like a chess-man beside him. As for the residue of the Pequod’s company, be it said, that at the present day not one in two of the many thousand men before the mast employed in the American whale fishery, are Americans born, though pretty nearly all the officers are. Herein it is the same with the American whale fishery as with the American army and military and merchant navies, and the engineering forces employed in the construction of the American Canals and Railroads. The same, I say, because in all these cases the native American liberally provides the brains, the rest of the world as generously supplying the muscles. No small number of these whaling seamen belong to the Azores, where the outward bound Nantucket whalers frequently touch to augment their crews from the hardy peasants of those rocky shores. In like manner, the Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London, put in at the Shetland Islands, to receive the full complement of their crew. Upon the passage homewards, they drop them there again. How it is, there is no telling, but Islanders seem to make the best whalemen. They were nearly all Islanders in the Pequod, Isolatoes too, I call such, not acknowledging the common continent of men, but each Isolato living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, federated along one keel, what a set these Isolatoes were! An Anacharsis Clootz deputation from all the isles of the sea, and all the ends of the earth, accompanying Old Ahab in the Pequod to lay the world’s grievances before that bar from which not very many of them ever come back. Black Little Pip—he never did—oh, no! he went before. Poor Alabama boy! On the grim Pequod’s forecastle, ye shall ere long see him, beating his tambourine; prelusive of the eternal time, when sent for, to the great quarter-deck on high, he was bid strike in with angels, and beat his tambourine in glory; called a coward here, hailed a hero there!

modern_da.title: Kapitel 27 — Riddere og væbnere
paragraphs: Stubb var anden styrmand. Han kom fra Cape Cod og blev derfor efter lokal skik kaldt en Cape-Cod-mand. Han var sorgløs og tog tingene, som de kom, ikke kujon og ikke helt, og han mødte farerne, efterhånden som de kom, med en mine af ligegyldighed; og i jagtens allerstrammeste øjeblik arbejdede han videre, rolig og fattet, som en svend i snedkerfaget, der er ansat på årsbasis. Han var godmodig, afslappet og ubekymret, og han styrede sin hvalbåd, som om det dødeligste møde kun var et middagsselskab og hans mandskab alle indbudte gæster. Han var lige så omhyggelig med at indrette sin ende af båden bekvemt, som en gammel postvognskusk er med, hvor lunt hans sæde er. Når han var helt tæt på hvalen, i selve dødsgrebet i kampen, håndterede han sin ubarmhjertige lanse køligt og skødesløst, som en fløjtende kedelflikker håndterer sin hammer. Han nynnede sine gamle rigadig-melodier, mens han lå side om side med det mest rasende uhyre. For denne Stubb havde lang vane gjort dødens gab til en god lænestol. Hvad han tænkte om selve døden, kan ingen sige. Om han nogensinde tænkte på den overhovedet, kunne være et rimeligt spørgsmål; men hvis han nogensinde skulle have vendt sit sind den vej efter en god middag, så tog han det uden tvivl, som en god sømand, som en slags vagtkald om at tumle op i masten og få travlt dér med noget, han ville finde ud af, hvad var, når han adlød ordren, og ikke før.

Hvad der måske, sammen med andre ting, gjorde Stubb til sådan en sorgløs, uforfærdet mand, der gik så glad og muntert med livets byrde i en verden fuld af alvorlige bærehandlere, alle bøjet mod jorden af deres bylter — hvad der var med til at skabe hans næsten gudløse gode humør — det må have været hans pibe. For ligesom hans næse var hans korte, sorte lille pibe et af de faste træk i hans ansigt. Man ville næsten lige så snart have ventet, at han kom ud af sin køje uden sin næse som uden sin pibe. Han havde en hel række piber derinde, stoppede og klare, stukket i et stativ lige inden for rækkevidde; og hver gang han gik til køjs, røg han dem alle ud efter hinanden, tændte hver ny ved den forrige helt til enden, og stoppede dem så igen, så de var klare endnu en gang. For når Stubb klædte sig på, satte han ikke først benene i bukserne, men piben i munden.

Jeg siger, at denne uafbrudte rygning må have været i det mindste én årsag til hans ejendommelige temperament. For alle ved, at den jordiske luft, både på land og til søs, er frygtelig smittet med de utallige menneskers navnløse elendighed, som har åndet den ind og er døde. Og ligesom nogle mennesker under et koleraudbrud går rundt og presser kamferdryppede lommetørklæder mod munden, således kan Stubbs tobaksrøg mod alle dødelige genvordigheder have tjent som en slags desinfektion.

Tredje styrmand var Flask, født i Tisbury på Martha's Vineyard. En lav, tyk, rødmusset ung fyr, meget kamplysten over for hvaler, som på en eller anden måde syntes at mene, at de store leviatanner personligt og arveligt havde fornærmet ham; og derfor var det en slags æressag for ham at ødelægge dem, hver gang han mødte dem. Han var så fuldstændig blottet for enhver følelse af ærefrygt for de mange vidundere i deres majestætiske størrelse og mystiske færden, og så døv for enhver fornemmelse af mulig fare ved at møde dem, at den vidunderlige hval efter hans ringe mening kun var en slags forstørret mus, eller i det mindste vandrotte, som kun krævede lidt overlistelse og en lille smule tid og besvær for at blive dræbt og kogt. Denne uvidende, ubevidste uforfærdethed gjorde ham en smule lun på emnet hvaler; han fulgte disse fisk for sjov; og en treårig rejse rundt om Kap Horn var bare en munter spøg, som varede så længe. Ligesom en tømrers søm deles i smedede søm og skårne søm, kan menneskeheden deles på samme måde. Lille Flask var en af de smedede, lavet til at sidde fast og holde længe. De kaldte ham Kongestolpe om bord på Pequod, fordi han i form kunne sammenlignes med det korte, firkantede tømmer, der går under det navn på arktiske hvalfangere, og som ved hjælp af mange udstrålende sidetømmer, der er sat ind i det, tjener til at afstive skibet mod de isnende stød fra de hærgende have.

Nu var disse tre styrmænd — Starbuck, Stubb og Flask — vigtige mænd. Efter almindelig tradition førte de som bådførere kommandoen over tre af Pequods både. I den store slagorden, som kaptajn Ahab sandsynligvis ville opstille sine styrker i for at gå ned mod hvalerne, var disse tre bådførere som kompagnichefer. Eller, bevæbnet med deres lange, skarpe hvallanser, var de et udvalgt trekløver af lansenérer, ligesom harpunererne var spydkastere.

Og eftersom hver styrmand eller bådfører i dette berømte fangstfag, som en gotisk ridder fra gamle dage, altid ledsages af sin bådstyrer eller harpunér, der på visse øjeblikke rækker ham en ny lanse, når den første er blevet slemt vredet eller bøjet i et knæ under angrebet; og eftersom der desuden som regel findes et nært venskab og fortrolighed mellem de to, er det kun passende, at vi her nedskriver, hvem Pequods harpunerer var, og hvilken bådfører hver af dem hørte til.
Først var Queequeg, som Starbuck, første styrmand, havde valgt som sin væbner. Men Queequeg kender vi allerede.

Dernæst var Tashtego, en ublandet indianer fra Gay Head, det vestligste forbjerg på Martha's Vineyard, hvor der stadig findes den sidste rest af en landsby af rødhuder, som i lang tid har leveret mange af sine dristigste harpunerer til naboøen Nantucket. I fangsten går de sædvanligvis under det fælles navn Gay Headere. Tashtegos lange, magre, sortbrune hår, hans høje kindben og hans sorte, runde øjne — for en indianer orientalske i deres størrelse, men antarktiske i deres glitrende udtryk — alt dette var nok til at forkynde ham som arving til det uforfalskede blod fra de stolte krigerjægere, der på jagt efter den store New England-elg havde gennemstrejfet fastlandets urskove med buen i hånden. Men nu snuste Tashtego ikke længere efter skovens vilde dyrs spor; han jagede i kølvandet på havets store hvaler, og sønnens usvigelige harpun afløste på passende vis fædrenes ufejlbarlige pil. Når man så på den gyldenbrune styrke i hans smidige, slangeagtige lemmer, ville man næsten have troet på nogle af de tidligere puritaneres overtro og halvvejs have troet, at denne vilde indianer var en søn af Luftens Magters Fyrste. Tashtego var væbner for Stubb, anden styrmand.

Den tredje blandt harpunererne var Daggoo, en kæmpestor, kulsort vilde med en løves gang — en Ahasverus at se til. I ørerne hang han to gyldne ringe, så store, at sømændene kaldte dem ringbolte og talte om, at man kunne gøre mærsfaldene fast i dem. I sin ungdom var Daggoo af egen fri vilje gået ombord på et hvalfangerskib, der lå i en ensom bugt på hans hjemlige kyst. Han havde aldrig været andre steder i verden end Afrika, Nantucket og de hedenske havne, som hvalfangerne oftest besøger. Nu havde han i mange år ført det dristige liv i fangsten på skibe, hvis redere var usædvanlig nøjeregnende med, hvilken slags folk de hyrede. Derfor havde Daggoo bevaret alle sine vilde dyder. Rank som en giraf gik han rundt på dækkene med al den pragt, der kan være i seks fod og fem tommer i strømpesokkerne. Der lå en legemlig ydmyghed i at se op på ham; og en hvid mand, der stod foran ham, lignede et hvidt flag, som er kommet for at tigge om våbenhvile hos en fæstning. Mærkeligt nok var denne kejserlige sorte mand, Ahasverus Daggoo, væbner for lille Flask, som tog sig ud som en skakbrik ved siden af ham. Hvad resten af Pequods mandskab angår, så lad det være sagt, at i vore dage er ikke engang halvdelen af de mange tusind mand, der gør tjeneste for masten i den amerikanske hvalfangst, født i Amerika, selv om næsten alle officererne er. I den henseende er den amerikanske hvalfangst som den amerikanske hær, den militære og den civile flåde og de ingeniørstyrker, der bygger Amerikas kanaler og jernbaner. Det samme, siger jeg, fordi den indfødte amerikaner i alle disse tilfælde gavmildt leverer hjernerne, mens resten af verden ligeså gavmildt leverer musklerne. Ikke så få af disse hvalfangere kommer fra Azores, hvor de udgående hvalfangere fra Nantucket ofte lægger til for at fylde mandskabet op med de hårdføre bønder fra de stenede kyster. På samme måde løber grønlandsfarerne fra Hull eller London ind til Shetlandsøerne for at få deres fulde besætning og sætter dem af igen samme sted på hjemvejen. Hvorfor det er sådan, kan ingen sige, men øboer ser ud til at blive de bedste hvalfangere. På Pequod var de næsten alle øboer — Isolatoer, som jeg kalder dem, fordi de ikke vil kendes ved menneskenes fælles fastland, men hver især bor på sit eget kontinent. Og alligevel, nu forenet på én køl, hvad var det ikke for en flok, disse Isolatoer! En Anacharsis Clootz-deputation fra alle verdenshavets øer og fra jordens yderste ender, som fulgte gamle Ahab på Pequod for at lægge verdens klager frem for den ret, hvorfra ikke ret mange af dem nogensinde vender tilbage. Lille sorte Pip — han gjorde aldrig — å nej! han gik forud. Stakkels dreng fra Alabama! På det dystre Pequods mandskabsrum skal I snart se ham slå på sit tamburin; en forsmag på den evige tid, da han, kaldt op på det store agterdæk i det høje, fik besked om at spille med englene og slå sit tamburin i herlighed; kaldt kujon her, hyldet som helt der!
